_comment: Shipped defaults. Do not edit this file -- it documents the full schema and is the
reference the validator checks against. Put your overrides in config.json, which is
deep-merged on top of this (objects merge; arrays REPLACE, so you can remove a default
STUN server rather than only add to it). Secrets belong in environment variables, not
in a JSON file that might get shared: see the STREAMER_* overrides in docs/SETUP.md.
The quality preset ladder is NOT here. It lives in public/shared/quality-math.js so the
browser and the server read the identical definitions; duplicating it into config would
create a second source of truth for the numbers the encoder is driven by.

_hostComment: The host role survives an accidental reload: on socket loss a grace timer runs, and a
rejoin carrying the matching hostToken reclaims it. Reclaim is evaluated on the join
itself, not on a janitor tick, so the deadline is exact.
A host who clicks Leave is promoting immediately -- the grace window exists for
unexpected socket loss, not for a deliberate exit, and waiting 30s would leave the room
with nobody able to end the session.
emptyRoomGraceMs MUST exceed hostGraceMs, and the validator enforces it: a solo host's
own reload empties the room, and if empty-room cleanup ran first the room would be
deleted before the page finished loading, making the whole reclaim mechanism dead code.

_iceComment: STUN is a third party by design: each browser sends UDP binding requests to these
servers, which discloses its public IP and the session timing to whoever runs them.
That is the cost of discovering your own address behind NAT. Set iceServers to [] for
a LAN-only deployment, where host candidates connect without any of this.
TURN is off by default because enabling it routes media through a relay -- the one
thing this app otherwise never does.

_budgetComment: Total outbound video budget, divided by the number of REMOTE peers you send to
(participants - 1), never by the participant count. At the default 4-participant cap
that is 20000/3 = 6.67 Mbps per peer, which is what makes the 1080p60 default (6 Mbps)
reachable. The two numbers were chosen together.
20 Mbps is a LAN or fibre figure. On residential upstream -- often 1-5 Mbps -- it is
far above the real link, which makes the clamp inert exactly where it was meant to
help: the encoder saturates the uplink and takes the signaling socket and the audio
down with it until adaptation reacts. Two mitigations, both on by default: the lobby
exposes this as an editable 'Your upload speed', and bandwidth-triggered step-downs
use a shorter window than CPU-triggered ones so saturation is measured in seconds.
Set it to your actual measured upload speed. It is the single most useful number to
_adaptComment: Consecutive 1-second samples of a limitation reason before stepping down one rung.
Bandwidth reacts faster than CPU because a saturated uplink degrades everything on the
link, including the WebSocket; a busy CPU only degrades the video.
Raising is never automatic -- the UI suggests it and the user decides.
adaptWarmupMs ignores everything for the first seconds of a new video track. During
that window the encoder is still ramping and the send rate is legitimately far below
the cap while qualityLimitationReason reads 'bandwidth' -- the estimator probing, not
congestion. Adapting on it permanently downgrades a call that was about to be healthy.

_comment: echoCancellation is off because the usual setup is headphones, and AEC mangles the
system audio of whatever is being shared. Turn it on if you use speakers.
stdout only, never a file. SDP and ICE candidates are never logged even at debug: they
contain network topology, and this app has no reason to retain any of it.
